warmup.q: 2,000 virtual threads on JDK 21 are each blocked in socket.getInputStream().read(). Roughly how many platform threads does the JVM have?
options: About 2,000: each blocked read still needs an OS thread underneath
About 15: the carriers (one per core), a few JDK poller threads, and the JVM's own threads
Exactly 4: the carriers do all the waiting
About 1,000: the JDK pairs two virtual threads per OS thread
warmup.why: A blocked virtual thread is parked, not running, and it holds no OS thread. The JDK registers each socket with an internal poller that waits in epoll_wait, so the only extra platform threads are the poller threads. This lesson's demo counted 14 platform threads for 2,000 blocked readers on JDK 21: 4 carriers, Read-Poller, Write-Poller, two updater threads and JVM housekeeping.

sections.h: Zero-copy: let the kernel move the file
sections.html:
Sending a file the obvious way passes every byte through your process twice. read copies bytes from the kernel's page cache (its in-memory copy of recently used file pages) into your buffer, and write copies them back into the kernel's socket send buffer. With a heap ByteBuffer, the JDK adds another copy through a temporary direct buffer, as lesson 2 showed. Each call is also a system call: a switch from your program into the kernel and back.

FileChannel.transferTo asks the kernel to do the whole move. On Linux, with a socket as the target, the JDK uses sendfile(2): the kernel sends pages from the page cache straight to the socket, and the bytes never enter your process. A run for this track sent 64 MiB to a loopback socket and counted system calls with strace:

transferTo:                            sendfile 1 call
copy through a 64 KiB heap buffer:     read 2,119 calls, write 1,037 calls, no sendfile
                                       (the reads include the receiving side)

Like write on a non-blocking socket, transferTo may move fewer bytes than you asked for. It returns how many it moved, so it lives in a loop:

Java
long sent = 0;
while (sent < count) {
    sent += file.transferTo(position + sent, count - sent, socket);   // maybe partial
}
Kotlin
var sent = 0L
while (sent < count) {
    sent += file.transferTo(position + sent, count - sent, socket)   // maybe partial
}

Netty wraps the same idea in DefaultFileRegion: write one to a channel and the transport sends the file. The NIO transport calls FileChannel.transferTo, and the native epoll transport calls sendfile itself. When the socket buffer fills, sendfile fails with EAGAIN ("try again later"), and Netty waits for writability and resumes: lesson 2's partial-write logic again.

Zero-copy has one condition: the bytes must leave exactly as they sit in the file. If the JVM encrypts them with TLS or compresses them, that work happens in your process, so the bytes have to come up into user space anyway. Tomcat's connector docs show the trade-off: for static files over 48 KiB it uses sendfile and skips compression. In payments, that makes zero-copy a tool for bulk transfers over plain internal links, such as settlement files and statement exports, where TLS ends at a proxy in front of the JVM.

try.title: Count the system calls
steps: Run ZeroCopyDemo (or ZeroCopyDemoKt) with the command below. It sends a 64 MiB file twice: with transferTo, then through a 64 KiB heap buffer.
Before looking at the times, predict how many transferTo calls the first pass makes.
On Linux with strace, run it outside Gradle: strace -f -c -e trace=sendfile,read,write java -cp nio/build/classes/java/demo workbench.nio.l08.ZeroCopyDemo, and find the sendfile line.

code.title: ZeroCopyDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.nio.l08; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.RandomAccessFile; import java.net.InetAddress; import java.net.InetSocketAddress; import java.nio.ByteBuffer; import java.nio.channels.FileChannel; import java.nio.channels.ServerSocketChannel; import java.nio.channels.SocketChannel; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; /** Sends a file over a loopback socket twice: FileChannel.transferTo (zero-copy) and read/write through a heap buffer. Arg: MiB (default 64). */ public class ZeroCopyDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { long size = (args.length > 0 ? Long.parseLong(args[0]) : 64) << 20; Path file = Files.createTempFile("statement", ".bin"); try (RandomAccessFile raf = new RandomAccessFile(file.toFile(), "rw")) { raf.setLength(size); } try { for (String mode : new String[] {"transferTo", "copy"}) send(file, size, mode); } finally { Files.delete(file); } } static void send(Path file, long size, String mode) throws Exception { try (ServerSocketChannel listener = ServerSocketChannel.open() .bind(new InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0))) { Thread receiver = new Thread(() -> { // drains the socket, counts bytes try (SocketChannel in = listener.accept()) { ByteBuffer b = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(1 << 20); while (in.read(b) >= 0) b.clear(); } catch (IOException e) { e.printStackTrace(); } }); receiver.start(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); int calls = 0; try (FileChannel f = FileChannel.open(file); SocketChannel out = SocketChannel.open(listener.getLocalAddress())) { if (mode.equals("transferTo")) { long sent = 0; while (sent < size) { // may move less than asked: loop sent += f.transferTo(sent, size - sent, out); calls++; } } else { ByteBuffer b = ByteBuffer.allocate(64 * 1024); // heap: the JDK copies it again, via a direct buffer while (f.read(b) >= 0) { b.flip(); while (b.hasRemaining()) out.write(b); b.clear(); calls++; } } } receiver.join(); System.out.printf("%-10s %d MiB in %4d ms, %,d %s calls%n", mode, size >> 20, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, calls, mode.equals("copy") ? "read" : "transferTo"); } } }

try.expect: One transferTo call for all 64 MiB on loopback, against 1,024 read calls for the copy. The times are close and change from run to run (40 to 46 ms against 41 to 44 ms here), so a single run proves nothing about speed. strace shows the real difference: 1 sendfile call, against about a thousand write calls and twice as many read calls for the copying pass.

sections.h: Readiness or completion: epoll and io_uring
sections.html:
Everything in this track so far uses readiness notification. epoll answers "which sockets are ready?", and then your loop makes the read or write system call itself: one call to wait, and one more per socket to move bytes.

io_uring is a newer Linux interface that works by completion instead. Your program and the kernel share two ring buffers in memory. You put requests on the submission ring, such as "read up to 16 KiB from this socket into this buffer", the kernel does the work, and it puts results on the completion ring: "done, 4,096 bytes". One system call can submit and collect many operations, and the kernel, not your thread, moves the bytes.

On the JVM you reach io_uring through Netty; the JDK's own selector and poller use epoll. Netty 4.2 moved io_uring out of the incubator into a first-class transport. Its package is io.netty.channel.uring, and you use it like the other transports: a MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup with IoUringIoHandler.newFactory(), and the IoUring channel classes. Netty checks the kernel when it loads, and IoUring.isAvailable() says whether it can run on this machine.

Is it faster? Not reliably. This section's demo sends a 32 MiB DefaultFileRegion over every transport available:

nio      received 33,554,432 bytes in 29 ms
epoll    received 33,554,432 bytes in 18 ms
kqueue   unavailable: java.lang.ExceptionInInitializerError
io_uring received 33,554,432 bytes in 65 ms

The research for this track saw the same order (86 ms for epoll, 159 ms for io_uring in one run). Under strace, io_uring made no sendfile calls at all; the work went through 2,061 io_uring_enter calls, and Netty's history shows that it splices a file region instead. The transport is also still changing: Netty 4.2.20 itself contains several io_uring fixes. So measure your own workload before you switch. The switch is small, one factory and one channel class, which makes it cheap to try and cheap to undo.

steps: Predict which transports your machine supports: Linux has epoll and maybe io_uring; macOS has kqueue.

sections.h: Under a virtual thread's blocking read: the JDK's own event loop
sections.html:
When a virtual thread calls socket.getInputStream().read() and no bytes have arrived, no OS thread blocks. The JDK's sources and a thread dump show what happens instead:

  1. The JDK's socket implementation, NioSocketImpl, keeps the socket in non-blocking mode, so the read returns at once with EAGAIN: nothing yet.
  2. It registers the socket's file descriptor with an internal Poller, which uses epoll with EPOLLONESHOT (report once, then disarm), and parks the virtual thread. Its carrier, the platform thread that was running it, moves on to other virtual threads.
  3. A poller thread waits in epoll_wait on every registered socket. When data arrives, it unparks the virtual thread, which is mounted on a free carrier and tries the read again.

A jcmd thread dump of a parked reader shows that path: NioSocketImpl.read, then NioSocketImpl.park, Poller.poll, LockSupport.park and VirtualThread.park.

Which threads do the polling depends on the JDK version. On JDK 21 the pollers are platform threads named Read-Poller and Write-Poller, plus Read-Updater and Write-Updater on Linux. This section's demo, on JDK 21, with 2,000 virtual threads blocked in read():

2000 virtual threads blocked in read(); platform threads: 14
   4 x ForkJoinPool-N-worker-N
   1 x Read-Poller
   1 x Read-Updater
   1 x Write-Poller
   1 x Write-Updater
   ...
wrote 1 byte to each socket: all 2,000 readers woke and finished in 36 ms

From JDK 22, Linux defaults to a mode the JDK source calls VTHREAD_POLLERS: one platform MasterPoller thread plus sub-pollers that are themselves virtual threads, scheduled like any other, which the source says "helps to integrate polling with virtual thread scheduling". That is the default on Linux in JDK 25, the current LTS; macOS keeps platform poller threads. From JDK 24, jcmd <pid> Thread.vthread_pollers lists the pollers.

So virtual threads don't make event loops obsolete. They put one inside the JDK, so your code can stay blocking-style while an epoll loop does the waiting.

try.title: Find the pollers
steps: Run PollerDemo (or PollerDemoKt). Predict the number of platform threads before you look.
Run it with -Pargs=5000 and predict again: which names grow, if any?

If you have JDK 25 installed, run the class with it directly: java -cp nio/build/classes/java/demo workbench.nio.l08.PollerDemo 2000 30, and while it holds, run jcmd <pid> Thread.vthread_pollers with the pid it prints. Which poller names appear?

code.title: PollerDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.nio.l08; import java.io.IOException; import java.net.InetAddress; import java.net.ServerSocket; import java.net.Socket; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.TreeMap; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.stream.Collectors; /** * N virtual threads each block in Socket.read(). Which platform threads exist meanwhile? * Args: [N, default 2000] [seconds to hold before releasing them, default 0] */ public class PollerDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int n = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 2_000; int holdSeconds = args.length > 1 ? Integer.parseInt(args[1]) : 0; System.out.println("java " + System.getProperty("java.version") + ", cpus=" + Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() + ", pid=" + ProcessHandle.current().pid()); try (ServerSocket server = new ServerSocket(0, n, InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress()); ExecutorService readers = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { CountDownLatch connected = new CountDownLatch(n), done = new CountDownLatch(n); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { readers.submit(() -> { try (Socket s = new Socket(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), server.getLocalPort())) { connected.countDown(); s.getInputStream().read(); // parks this virtual thread on the JDK poller } catch (IOException e) { e.printStackTrace(); } finally { done.countDown(); } }); } List<Socket> accepted = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) accepted.add(server.accept()); connected.await(); Thread.sleep(300); // let every reader reach read() Map<String, Long> platform = Thread.getAllStackTraces().keySet().stream() // platform threads only .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(t -> t.getName().replaceAll("\\d+", "N"), TreeMap::new, Collectors.counting())); System.out.println(n + " virtual threads blocked in read(); platform threads: " + platform.values().stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum()); platform.forEach((name, count) -> System.out.println(" " + count + " x " + name)); if (holdSeconds > 0) { System.out.println("holding " + holdSeconds + " s: try jcmd " + ProcessHandle.current().pid() + " Thread.dump_to_file -format=json dump.json"); Thread.sleep(holdSeconds * 1_000L); } long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (Socket s : accepted) s.getOutputStream().write(1); // data arrives: the poller unparks each reader done.await(); System.out.printf("wrote 1 byte to each socket: all %,d readers woke and finished in %d ms%n", n, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); for (Socket s : accepted) s.close(); } } }

All readers wake within tens of milliseconds once data arrives. On JDK 25 on Linux, the platform list shows a MasterPoller instead of the read and write pollers and their updaters, because the sub-pollers are virtual threads and getAllStackTraces lists only platform threads; Thread.vthread_pollers shows them all. (The JDK 25 names come from the JDK source; this track ran its demos on JDK 21.)

sections.h: Choosing a server model for a payments service
sections.html:
After eight lessons the choice comes down to two questions: where does the waiting happen, and what limits it?

If the service... Choose Watch out for
uses JDBC, JTA and blocking SDKs, and is IO-bound thread-per-request on virtual threads: Quarkus @RunOnVirtualThread, Jetty's virtual threads executor a limit per downstream; pinning on JDK 21 to 23; CPU-heavy work
has the same blocking stack and moderate traffic a bounded worker pool: Quarkus plain endpoints, Jetty's QueuedThreadPool size it with Little's law; the pool caps concurrency
is async end to end (reactive SQL, async HTTP, streaming) an event loop: Vert.x, Netty, Quarkus Uni endpoints never block the loop; backpressure
holds many idle long-lived connections (terminals, WebSockets) an event loop, or virtual threads if the per-connection work blocks memory per connection; idle timeouts
sends large files unchanged zero-copy: transferTo, Netty's DefaultFileRegion no TLS or compression inside the JVM

Two rules hold in every row. Concurrency needs a limit somewhere. An event loop limits it by never waiting, and a pool by its size. With virtual threads you have to add one, because 10,000 parked threads will make 10,000 calls to your card issuer the moment they wake. The lab for this lesson is exactly that bug. And the model doesn't change latency: a 120 ms issuer call takes 120 ms in every row.

My default for a new payments service on Quarkus is plain blocking endpoints, moving to @RunOnVirtualThread when the worker pool becomes the limit, with JDBC and issuer calls behind explicit limits. Event loops and Uni earn their extra complexity when the whole stack is non-blocking or connection counts are very large. Whatever you choose, measure it: Little's law for threads, the lag probe and blocked-thread warnings for loops, and strace -c when you want to know what the kernel is really doing.

try.title: Choose for three services
steps: A card-present gateway keeps 8,000 TCP connections from terminals; each sends one 200-byte message a minute and the work per message is a 3 ms in-memory check. Choose a model.
A refund service: Quarkus, Oracle through JDBC with JTA, a blocking acquirer SDK at 400 ms, 150 requests a second at peak. Choose a model and say where the limits go.
A nightly job sends 2 GB settlement files to an internal archive over plain TCP. Choose how to send them.
try.expect: The gateway is almost all idle connections and tiny non-blocking work: an event loop (Netty or Vert.x) fits, with an idle timeout and framing as in lesson 4. The refund service needs 150 × 0.4 = 60 requests in flight: plain blocking endpoints on the worker pool work, or @RunOnVirtualThread; either way, put @Blocking on JTA endpoints that return Uni, cap the acquirer SDK with a semaphore, and size the JDBC pool on purpose. The settlement job is zero-copy territory: FileChannel.transferTo in a loop (or Netty's DefaultFileRegion), since nothing has to change the bytes on the way.

analogy: A virtual thread's blocking read is a coat check. The virtual thread hands the poller a ticket (the socket's file descriptor) and leaves the counter, so the carrier, the clerk, can serve the next person in line. When the coat arrives (data on the socket), the poller calls the ticket number, and whichever clerk is free hands the coat back. Zero-copy is the opposite of a coat check: the parcel never comes to the counter at all, the warehouse ships it straight to the door. The analogy breaks at speed: a real coat check is slow, while parking and unparking a virtual thread is cheap, which is why 2,000 readers woke in 36 ms in this lesson's demo.
world: Statement exports, settlement files and reconciliation reports are where zero-copy pays off in payments, provided TLS ends at the proxy or gateway in front of the JVM. For APIs, the choice of model matters more than the transport: most payment services are blocking stacks (Oracle, JDBC, JTA, vendor SDKs), and on JDK 21 or newer they can serve high concurrency on virtual threads, as long as every downstream sits behind an explicit limit. If your fleet still runs JDK 21, upgrading to the current LTS, JDK 25, brings both synchronized without pinning (JEP 491, from JDK 24) and virtual-thread pollers on Linux. Treat io_uring as an experiment to measure, not a default.
mistake: The common mistake is moving a blocking service to virtual threads and deleting the thread-pool limit with nothing in its place. The old pool of 200 threads was quietly protecting the database and the card issuer. Virtual threads remove that cap, so the next burst sends thousands of concurrent queries to a 20-connection pool or an issuer that allows 100 calls, and latency or error rates explode downstream. Put a Semaphore (or the client's own concurrency limit) around each fragile dependency, with a timeout on acquiring it, when you introduce virtual threads.

compare.title: A bounded zero-copy export on virtual threads

java.title: StatementServer.export, Java
java.html: private final Semaphore exportSlots = new Semaphore(maxConcurrentExports); // the database allows 4 void export(String day, SocketChannel out) throws Exception { exportSlots.acquire(); // waiting here parks the virtual thread try { Thread.sleep(QUERY_MILLIS); // the statement query try (FileChannel file = FileChannel.open(statements.resolve(day + ".csv"))) { FileSender.transferFully(file, 0, file.size(), out); // sendfile on Linux } } finally { exportSlots.release(); } }

kotlin.title: StatementServer.export, Kotlin
kotlin.html: private val exportSlots = Semaphore(maxConcurrentExports) // the database allows 4 fun export(day: String, out: SocketChannel) { exportSlots.acquire() // waiting here parks the virtual thread try { Thread.sleep(QUERY_MILLIS) // the statement query FileChannel.open(statements.resolve("$day.csv")).use { file -> FileSender.transferFully(file, 0, file.size(), out) // sendfile on Linux } } finally { exportSlots.release() } }

compare.note: Both use java.util.concurrent.Semaphore, and on a virtual thread acquire() parks without holding a carrier. A Kotlin team might reach for kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore with withPermit { } instead. That one only works inside coroutines and suspends rather than parks, so it fits a coroutine-based server, not this thread-per-connection one. FileChannel.transferTo is the same JDK call from both languages; Kotlin's use {} plays the part of Java's try-with-resources for the file channel.

steps.say: Requirements: at month end, 600 statement downloads a minute; each needs a 1.5 s database query and about 0.5 s to send its file. The database team allows 8 concurrent statement queries. Little's law first.
steps.code:
arrival rate     = 600 / 60 s           = 10 requests/s
time in system   = 1.5 s + 0.5 s        = 2 s
in flight        = 10 x 2               = 20 requests
queries at once  = capped at 8          -> requests wait for a slot, not for a thread

steps.say: Use one virtual thread per connection, so waiting for the query, for a slot or for a slow client costs no OS thread. Put the database's limit in a semaphore with a timeout, so an overloaded database turns into a fast error.
steps.code: private final Semaphore querySlots = new Semaphore(8); void export(String day, SocketChannel out) throws Exception { if (!querySlots.tryAcquire(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) { // 1. wait for a slot, but not forever throw new IllegalStateException("statement service busy"); } try { renderStatement(day); // 2. 1.5 s query, parks the virtual thread } finally { querySlots.release(); // 3. free the slot before the slow send } sendFile(day, out); }

alt.html: private val querySlots = Semaphore(8) fun export(day: String, out: SocketChannel) { if (!querySlots.tryAcquire(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) { // 1. wait for a slot, but not forever throw IllegalStateException("statement service busy") } try { renderStatement(day) // 2. 1.5 s query, parks the virtual thread } finally { querySlots.release() // 3. free the slot before the slow send } sendFile(day, out) }

steps.say: Send the file with zero-copy, in a loop, because transferTo can stop early when the client's socket is full. Releasing the query slot before this step matters: a slow client should hold a cheap virtual thread, not one of the 8 database slots.
steps.code: static int transferFully(FileChannel file, long position, long count, WritableByteChannel target) throws IOException { long sent = 0; int calls = 0; while (sent < count) { sent += file.transferTo(position + sent, count - sent, target); // may be partial calls++; } return calls; }

alt.html: fun transferFully(file: FileChannel, position: Long, count: Long, target: WritableByteChannel): Int { var sent = 0L var calls = 0 while (sent < count) { sent += file.transferTo(position + sent, count - sent, target) // may be partial calls++ } return calls }

steps.say: Check the conditions before you promise zero-copy. If TLS terminates inside the JVM, the bytes must be encrypted in user space and transferTo gives you no zero-copy; send through a buffer and stop worrying about it. If an ingress proxy terminates TLS, the JVM's socket is plain and sendfile applies. Either way, the design's real limit is the 8 query slots, not the transfer method.

lab.title: Export statements with zero-copy on virtual threads, within a limit
steps: Run the tests. Two of three fail. The idle-connection test already passes: read it, it shows 300 parked virtual threads costing almost no platform threads.

Write FileSender.transferFully: call file.transferTo in a loop until count bytes are sent, and return the number of calls. The first test feeds it a channel that accepts only 4 KiB per write, so a single call is never enough.
Run the tests. The download test now fails on concurrency: all 20 exports ran at once.
Fix StatementServer.export: add a java.util.concurrent.Semaphore with maxConcurrentExports permits, acquire() before measured { ... } and release() in a finally. Run the tests until all three pass.
hints: transferTo returns the number of bytes it moved this time; add it to the bytes sent so far and start the next call at position + sent.
Acquire the permit outside measured { }, so that threads waiting for a permit don't count as running exports.
Waiting in Semaphore.acquire() parks a virtual thread just like a socket read does: twenty waiting exports cost twenty parked virtual threads, not twenty OS threads.

drill.title: Write the transfer loop from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write transferFully(file, position, count, target) that sends count bytes of a FileChannel with transferTo, survives partial transfers and returns the number of calls. When does Linux turn it into sendfile, and when can't it be zero-copy?

answer.html: fun transferFully(file: FileChannel, position: Long, count: Long, target: WritableByteChannel): Int { var sent = 0L var calls = 0 while (sent < count) { sent += file.transferTo(position + sent, count - sent, target) // may be partial calls++ } return calls } // sendfile: when the target is a socket on Linux. // Not zero-copy when the bytes must be changed in the JVM first: TLS in the JVM, compression.

alt.html: static int transferFully(FileChannel file, long position, long count, WritableByteChannel target) throws IOException { long sent = 0; int calls = 0; while (sent < count) { sent += file.transferTo(position + sent, count - sent, target); // may be partial calls++; } return calls; } // sendfile: when the target is a socket on Linux. // Not zero-copy when the bytes must be changed in the JVM first: TLS in the JVM, compression.

recap: Copying a file to a socket passes each byte through your process; FileChannel.transferTo becomes sendfile(2) on Linux and keeps the bytes in the kernel. It can stop early, so call it in a loop.
Netty's DefaultFileRegion does zero-copy per transport. Zero-copy needs the bytes unchanged: TLS or compression inside the JVM rules it out.

epoll reports readiness and you make the IO call; io_uring takes requests on a shared ring and reports completions. Netty 4.2 supports io_uring as a first-class transport, and in this track's runs it was not faster.

A virtual thread's blocking socket read is a non-blocking read, a registration with the JDK's poller (EPOLLONESHOT) and a park. JDK 21 uses platform Read-Poller threads; JDK 22+ on Linux uses a MasterPoller plus virtual sub-pollers.
Pick the model by where waiting happens: virtual threads or a worker pool for blocking stacks, event loops for async stacks and huge idle connection counts, zero-copy for unchanged files.
Every model needs a concurrency limit somewhere; with virtual threads you add it yourself.

explain.prompt: A teammate says "we moved to virtual threads, so we don't need event loops anymore". Explain what happens inside the JDK when a virtual thread blocks on a socket read, and what still needs your attention.
explain.answer: When a virtual thread reads from a socket that has no data, the JDK's socket code does a non-blocking read, gets EAGAIN, registers the socket's file descriptor with an internal poller and parks the virtual thread. The carrier thread is free to run other virtual threads. A poller thread waits in epoll_wait on all registered sockets and unparks the virtual thread when data arrives. So there still is an event loop: it moved inside the JDK, which lets our code stay blocking-style. On JDK 21 the pollers are platform threads; from JDK 22 on Linux they are mostly virtual threads themselves. What still needs attention: virtual threads don't limit concurrency, so each downstream needs a semaphore or pool limit; pinning (synchronized before JDK 24, native code) and CPU-heavy work can hold carriers; and the requests still arrive on Netty event loops in Quarkus, which must never block.

deeper.html:
Dan Kegel's C10K page, from lesson 1, compared ways to serve many clients. This track has now met each family on the JVM: readiness notification with a level-triggered Selector (lesson 2) and Netty's native epoll transport (lessons 3 and 4); completion-based IO with io_uring (this lesson); and one thread per client with blocking IO, which virtual threads made cheap again by running a readiness loop underneath.

The JDK's poller has knobs, though you should rarely need them. On JDK 21, -Djdk.readPollers sets the number of read pollers (a power of 2, default 1); with 4, a thread dump shows four Read-Poller threads. From JDK 22, -Djdk.pollerMode selects the mode: 1 for SYSTEM_THREADS (platform pollers, the JDK 21 behavior) and 2 for VTHREAD_POLLERS. The JDK source after the current LTS adds a third mode, POLLER_PER_CARRIER (3), in JDK 27, while the Linux default stays VTHREAD_POLLERS. In VTHREAD_POLLERS mode on Linux, the number of read pollers defaults to the highest power of 2 not above the CPU count, capped at 32.

Two smaller facts complete the picture. The JDK's Selector registers sockets level-triggered, while the poller uses one-shot registration: a selector serves the same socket again and again, while the poller wakes exactly one parked thread exactly once. And file IO is different from socket IO: a virtual thread reading a file does not go through the poller. As the virtual threads track explained, file operations capture the carrier while they run, which is one more reason zero-copy file sending is worth knowing about.

To check any of this on your own JDK, jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json dump.json shows virtual threads and their stacks, and from JDK 24 jcmd <pid> Thread.vthread_pollers shows the pollers.
